design_detail: Systematic review with random-effects meta-analyses (PROSPERO CRD420251148669) of randomized controlled trials in adults in which protective behavioural strategies (PBS) were actively taught, prompted or reinforced: limiting or stopping drinking (for example drink limits), manner of drinking (for example pacing) and harm-reduction strategies (for example a designated driver), alone or inside multi-component interventions, against no intervention, assessment only, education or other behavioural interventions. 15 trials published 2007–2023, all in young adults, 13 at US universities. Separate pools of Hedges' g from post-intervention means at the longest follow-up for alcohol quantity (9 trials), drinking frequency (6), alcohol-related problems (7) and PBS use (6); influence diagnostics with sensitivity analyses; subgroups by follow-up (3 months or less versus more) and by the role of PBS in the intervention. Mediation and moderation summarized narratively.
can_establish: The average effect, mostly in US university students, of interventions that teach or prompt bundles of protective drinking strategies on self-reported drinking quantity, frequency, alcohol-related problems and strategy use, compared with a mix of control conditions.
cannot_establish: The effect of any single strategy such as eating, pacing or alternating drinks (no trial tested one strategy domain alone); effects in older, community, treatment or non-Western populations; effects on harms measured other than by self-report; whether strategies are the mechanism of change (mediation tested in six trials, with inconsistent results); or, in multi-component trials, whether the effect comes from the strategies or from the other components.

sample.recruitment: Database search of PubMed, Embase, Scopus, CINAHL and ProQuest from inception to December 2025, limited to peer-reviewed English articles, plus citation tracking, reference lists and earlier reviews (Methods 2.2–2.3, pp. 2–3). Participants of the included trials were mostly undergraduates aged 18 to 24 at US universities; one trial in Sweden (university) and one pilot in Australia (campus and social media) (Results 3.1, p. 3; Table 1, p. 6).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: individual or cluster RCTs in adults (18 or older) who reported alcohol use, in which PBS were a primary or clearly identifiable component directly delivered by instruction, skills training, practice or prompting, with at least one quantitative alcohol outcome. Excluded: trials in which PBS were only an outcome, correlate, mediator or moderator; interventions aimed at norms, attitudes, motivation or identity without delivering PBS; non-randomized designs; reviews, protocols, conference abstracts and other non-peer-reviewed reports; under-18s without separate adult data (Methods 2.2, pp. 2–3).
sample.demographics: Randomized sample sizes 45 to 9,277; mean ages about 18 to 23 (two trials of people turning 21; one up to age 35); 41% to 100% women; risk profiles from universal samples to heavy episodic drinkers, students in counselling and 21st-birthday drinkers (Table 1, p. 6). Editors' calculation from Table 1: 15,714 randomized and 6,587 analysed across the 15 trials.
sample.attrition: Trial-level attrition 0% to 95%, highest in large digital trials (p. 5; Table 1). At review level, 20 of 79 reports sought were not retrieved (12 full text unavailable, 8 abstract only) (Fig. 1, p. 4).
sample.selection_effects: English-language, peer-reviewed reports only, without trial registries or grey literature; 20 possibly relevant reports were not retrieved. The evidence comes almost entirely from young US university students, so community, older, clinical and non-Western drinkers are not represented, as the authors state (p. 11).

exposure.measurement: Self-reported drinking and problems in every trial (the authors list reliance on self-report as a limitation, p. 11); PBS use measured by self-report scales where assessed. The instrument behind each pooled outcome is not identified trial by trial.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not applicable to alcohol amounts. Interventions were mostly single-session or brief and digital (web feedback, email, SMS, smartphone apps, mailed postcards, interactive voice response); four had a face-to-face component; repeated formats ran from 3 days to 10 weeks (Results 3.2, p. 5; Table 2, p. 7).
exposure.polysubstance: Not addressed; other drug use is not reported for any included trial.

comparison.controls: Assessment only (4 trials), no intervention (1), active or attention controls (study skills, health education, alcohol education, electronic brochure, control app, self-monitoring, differently framed messages), and in three booster trials the same computer-delivered intervention without the PBS booster (Table 2, p. 7).
comparison.matching: Randomization within trials. Comparator types were pooled together without stratification.

outcomes.instruments: Pooled outcomes: alcohol quantity, drinking frequency, alcohol-related problems and PBS use, each as Hedges' g with 95% CI from post-intervention group means, SDs and sample sizes, standard errors converted to SDs (Methods 2.7, p. 3). Trial risk of bias with RoB 2 by two independent reviewers (Methods 2.5, p. 3; Fig. 2, p. 5). Publication bias by funnel plots, rank correlation and Egger's test where feasible (p. 3).
outcomes.validity_norms: Hedges' g corrects for small samples; negative values favour the intervention for alcohol outcomes and positive values for PBS use. Post-intervention values were pooled without adjustment for baseline.
outcomes.operationalization: Benefit was lower self-reported quantity, frequency or problems, or more self-reported PBS use, in the intervention arm at the longest follow-up, which ranged from 3 days to 12 months (Table 3, p. 8).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. 4 counts the primary pooled analyses; there are also 2 influence-based sensitivity analyses and subgroup analyses by follow-up and by role of PBS (reported in the text for at least 8 estimates; supplementary figures S6–S16 not read).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable. Screening, extraction, classification of PBS role and risk-of-bias assessment were each done by two independent reviewers with a third for disagreements (Methods 2.4–2.6, pp. 3).

analysis.effect_sizes: Random-effects (Jamovi 2.6.44, MAJOR module), one effect per trial per model. Quantity: g −0.05 (95% CI −0.13 to 0.02), p = 0.162, 9 trials, I² 22.0%, prediction interval −0.18 to 0.07. Frequency: g −0.09 (−0.17 to −0.02), p = 0.014, 6 trials, I² 11.85%, prediction interval −0.19 to 0.001. Alcohol-related problems: g −0.07 (−0.14 to 0.0007), p = 0.052, 7 trials, I² 0%; without Larimer et al. (2007) g −0.10 (−0.19 to −0.01), p = 0.034. PBS use: g 0.58 (−0.21 to 1.37), p = 0.152, 6 trials, I² 97.8%, prediction interval −1.47 to 2.63; without the O'Donnell et al. (2019) pilot g 0.23 (0.07 to 0.40), p = 0.005, I² 49.9% (pp. 6–7). Subgroups (p. 7; intervals and numbers of trials only in supplements): follow-up over 3 months, quantity g −0.12 (p = 0.004) and frequency g −0.13 (p = 0.003); no significant effect at 3 months or less; adjunct role, quantity g −0.10 (p = 0.040) and frequency g −0.13 (p < 0.001); core or primary role, no significant effect on quantity, problems g −0.11 (p = 0.091), PBS use g 0.91 (p = 0.128). No test of the difference between subgroups is reported.
analysis.preregistration_detail: PROSPERO CRD420251148669, described as prospectively registered (Methods 2.1, p. 2). The registry record was not read; the paper reports no deviations. The influence-based exclusions that produce the abstract's headline PBS-use estimate and the significant problems estimate are not described as prespecified; the subgroup analyses are.
analysis.selective_reporting: The abstract gives the PBS-use effect only after removal of an outlier (g 0.23) and calls the problems effect significant in sensitivity analysis, while both prespecified pooled estimates were non-significant (p. 1 versus p. 6). Subgroup estimates are reported without confidence intervals or numbers of trials. Which arms of multi-arm trials were compared is not stated.
analysis.power: Not formally assessed; the authors state that 6 to 9 trials per pool and fewer per subgroup limit power and make subgroup findings exploratory (Discussion 4.1, p. 11).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 15 trials, mostly of US university students, interventions that taught or prompted bundles of protective drinking strategies did not detectably change self-reported drinking quantity (g −0.05, −0.13 to 0.02), produced a very small reduction in drinking frequency (g −0.09, −0.17 to −0.02; prediction interval reaching 0.001) and a borderline reduction in alcohol-related problems (g −0.07, upper limit 0.0007, p = 0.052). Effects on reported strategy use were highly heterogeneous (I² 97.8%) and not significant until one pilot trial was removed. No trial isolated a single strategy; 14 of 15 trials were at some concerns or high risk of bias; mediation through strategy use was found in some trials and not others.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract's first result is the outlier-excluded effect on strategy use (g 0.23, p = 0.005), and it reports the problems effect as significant in sensitivity analysis; that analysis removed the largest and most precise trial, Larimer et al. (2007) (p. 6; Fig. 5, p. 9). The abstract and discussion say effects were greater at longer follow-up and when strategies were part of multi-component interventions (pp. 1, 10), but no between-subgroup test is reported, the subgroups differ in trial size and type, and three of the four adjunct trials paired the strategies with personalized normative feedback (Table 2, p. 7), so the larger effects cannot be credited to the strategies, a point the authors partly make (p. 10). The results section summarizes risk of bias as low to moderate (p. 5) although only one trial was low risk. The abstract's statements on alcohol outcomes (modest, no change in quantity, small reduction in frequency) and on mechanism (limited and inconsistent) match the results, and the discussion calls the subgroup findings exploratory.

timeline.event: Earliest included trial (Larimer et al., 2007, mailed personalized feedback with PBS, 1,488 students, 12-month follow-up), the largest weight in the problems pool.
Pearson (2013): critical review of PBS use among college students, cited as an earlier review mostly of observational evidence (card sc_pearson_2013).

Greń and Ostaszewski (2023), and Cox et al. (2024), a systematic review of associations between PBS and heavy drinking in young adults: earlier reviews cited as based largely on observational evidence; not read.
Latest included trial (Arazan et al., 2023, emailed e-card for students turning 21; 88% to 95% attrition).
This review: by the authors' account the first meta-analysis restricted to RCTs delivering PBS as an active component.

replication.where_it_stands: The only meta-analysis of randomized trials of taught or prompted protective drinking strategies on the reading lists; the BeforeDuring list records that no trial of any single strategy on its own was found, which this review confirms (no trial isolated a strategy domain). Its estimates rest on 6 to 9 trials per outcome in US students. Primary trials cited here were not read; claims should not cite them as independent support alongside this review.

funding.funder: Ratchadapiseksomphot Endowment Fund, Chulalongkorn University (The Review Article Grant; Grant No. RA68011) and the Research grant for Systematic reviews and Meta-analyses from the Faculty of Nursing, Chulalongkorn University (p. 11).
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors declare no conflicts of interest related to this work and state that the manuscript was completed independently of any commercial or financial relationships (pp. 11–12).
funding.affiliations_note: Authors from nursing faculties in Vietnam (Thai Nguyen) and Thailand (Chulalongkorn, Burapha). The authors state that ChatGPT 5.3 was used to improve clarity and readability, with the authors reviewing and editing the text (p. 11).

what_would_settle_it: Pre-registered factorial or dismantling randomized trials that test single strategies (for example eating before drinking, pacing, alternating with non-alcoholic drinks, arranging transport) against each other and against a common control, in non-student adults as well as students, with event-level and objectively verified outcomes, including injuries and other harms, and follow-up beyond 6 months.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Population (adults who drink), intervention (actively delivered PBS), comparators and outcomes specified (pp. 2–3).

Prospectively registered on PROSPERO (p. 2); the registry record was not read and the paper does not compare its methods with the protocol or report deviations; the role classification was developed for this review.
RCTs only, justified as a more rigorous test than the observational evidence of earlier reviews (pp. 2, 10).

Five databases, citation and reference-list searching, strategy in Appendix 1 (not read); but limited to peer-reviewed English articles without a stated reason, and no trial registries or grey literature. Applied as written per senior decision 21 (2026-10-25).
Titles, abstracts and full texts screened independently by two reviewers (p. 3).
Independent extraction by two reviewers with a piloted form (p. 3).

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: Provisional: reasons for exclusion are said to be documented in Appendix 2 (p. 3), which is a supplement not among the files; the PRISMA diagram gives only counts by reason (Fig. 1, p. 4).

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Tables 1–3 give country, setting, design, randomized and analysed numbers, sex, age, risk profile, attrition, content, delivery, intensity, role, comparator, outcomes and follow-up (pp. 6–8); the instrument behind each pooled outcome is not identified.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: RoB 2 in duplicate with domain-level judgments for every trial (Fig. 2, p. 5); reasons for the judgments are not given, and the missing-data judgment for Arazan et al. (2023) looks lenient (see reporting issues).

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported

domains.note: Random-effects pooling of Hedges' g with one effect per trial, I², prediction intervals and influence diagnostics (p. 3). A close call: the handling of multi-arm trials is not described, assessment-only, active and booster-design comparators are pooled together, and a pool with I² of 97.8% is summarized by one estimate (with its prediction interval).

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: No risk-of-bias sensitivity analysis; the authors say it was not feasible because only one trial was low risk (p. 3).

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: A close call: the limitations state that high-risk trials were retained without sensitivity analysis and the estimates should be read cautiously, and discuss attrition, self-report and adherence (pp. 11); but the results describe overall risk of bias as low to moderate and miscount the high-risk trials (p. 5), and the abstract does not mention risk of bias.
Q, I² and prediction intervals reported, influence analyses run, and heterogeneity of PBS use discussed (pp. 6–7, 10).

Funnel plots, rank correlation and Egger's test for every pool, with no asymmetry found (p. 6; plots in supplementary figures S1–S4, not read). With 6 to 9 trials per pool these tests have little power, which the paper does not note.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Review funding and author declarations reported (pp. 11–12).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Provisional: one critical item is not met (item 4: English and peer-reviewed limits without justification, no registries or grey literature), which gives low confidence under the AMSTAR 2 rules; item 7 could not be judged without Appendix 2, and if that appendix lists no excluded studies with reasons the rating becomes critically low. Items 11 and 13 are close calls; a 'no' on either would also give critically low confidence. Otherwise the review is registered, duplicated at every step, uses RoB 2 and reports prediction intervals. Citable for: pooled effects of PBS-teaching interventions in mostly US students (no detectable effect on quantity; a very small effect on frequency; a borderline effect on problems; heterogeneous effects on strategy use) and for the absence of any trial of a single strategy. Not citable for: effects of any individual strategy such as eating before drinking, effects outside student populations, or strategies being the mechanism of change.

key_findings.finding: 15 RCTs published 2007–2023 were included: 13 in the United States and one each in Sweden and Australia, nearly all at universities, with randomized samples of 45 to 9,277; participants were mainly undergraduates aged 18 to 24 and attrition ranged from 0% to 95%.
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation from Table 1: 15,714 randomized and 6,587 analysed in total.

key_findings.finding: Searches of PubMed, Embase, Scopus, CINAHL and ProQuest from inception to December 2025 were limited to peer-reviewed English articles; after removing 58 duplicates, 456 records were screened, 79 reports sought, 20 not retrieved (12 full text unavailable, 8 abstract only), 59 assessed and 14 included, plus 1 of 12 found by reference and citation searching.
key_findings.note: The flow-chart counts are in Fig. 1, a drawing without a text layer; they were read from the rendered page.

key_findings.finding: No trial evaluated a single PBS domain in isolation, so effects of individual strategies could not be analysed; 11 interventions are said to have combined limiting, manner-of-drinking and harm-reduction strategies and 4 emphasized selective avoidance and alternatives.
key_findings.note: Table 2 shows two of the eleven (Andersson 2015; Arazan 2023) with only two of the three domains; see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: PBS had a core role in 4 trials, a primary role in 4, a booster role in 3 and an adjunct role (inside multi-component interventions, often with personalized normative feedback) in 4; most interventions were single-session or brief and digital, and four had a face-to-face component.

Risk of bias (RoB 2): one trial low risk in all domains (Martens et al., 2013); Fig. 2 shows four trials at high risk overall (Arazan 2023; Braitman and Henson 2016; Braitman and Lau-Barraco 2018; Dvorak 2015) and the remaining ten at some concerns; concerns arose mainly from deviations from intended interventions and missing outcome data.
key_findings.note: The text says three trials were high risk; the figure shows four. Trial names and judgments were read from Fig. 2, an image.

key_findings.finding: Alcohol quantity: pooled g −0.05 (95% CI −0.13 to 0.02), p = 0.162, 9 trials, I² 22.0%, 95% prediction interval −0.18 to 0.07; no influential outliers or publication bias detected.
key_findings.note: Fig. 3 (p. 9, image): trial estimates range from −0.54 (Leeman 2016) to +0.30 (Sugarman and Carey 2009, more drinking in the intervention arm, not significant); values read from the figure.

key_findings.finding: Drinking frequency: pooled g −0.09 (95% CI −0.17 to −0.02), p = 0.014, 6 trials, I² 11.85%, 95% prediction interval −0.19 to 0.001.
Alcohol-related problems: pooled g −0.07 (95% CI −0.14 to 0.0007), p = 0.052, 7 trials, I² 0%; after excluding Larimer et al. (2007), flagged as influential, g −0.10 (−0.19 to −0.01), p = 0.034.
key_findings.note: Fig. 5 (p. 9, image): Larimer 2007 is the largest-weight trial with g −0.03 (−0.13 to 0.07); value read from the figure.

key_findings.finding: PBS use: pooled g 0.58 (95% CI −0.21 to 1.37), p = 0.152, 6 trials, I² 97.8%, 95% prediction interval −1.47 to 2.63; after removing the outlier O'Donnell et al. (2019), g 0.23 (0.07 to 0.40), p = 0.005, I² 49.9%.
key_findings.locator: Results 3.4.4 (starts p. 6, I² after removal on p. 7)
key_findings.note: Fig. 6 (p. 10, image): O'Donnell 2019, a 45-person pilot, g 2.89 (1.97 to 3.80); value read from the figure.

key_findings.finding: Subgroups: with follow-up over 3 months, quantity g −0.12 (p = 0.004) and frequency g −0.13 (p = 0.003), with no significant effect at 3 months or less; with PBS as an adjunct, quantity g −0.10 (p = 0.040) and frequency g −0.13 (p < 0.001); with PBS as core or primary component, no significant effect on quantity, problems g −0.11 (p = 0.091), PBS use g 0.91 (p = 0.128). No test of differences between subgroups is reported.
key_findings.note: Intervals and numbers of trials per subgroup are only in supplementary figures S6–S16 (not read).

key_findings.finding: At trial level, 11 of 15 trials reported increased, maintained or mixed improvements in PBS use; 6 reported clear reductions in drinking, 1 partial and 1 mixed; 3 reported reductions in alcohol-related harms (one only after adjusting for consumption).

Mechanism: 6 trials ran mediation analyses, with significant indirect effects through PBS in three according to the text; 3 trials examined moderation, one finding stronger effects in people with lower baseline PBS use.
key_findings.locator: Results 3.3, 3rd paragraph (p. 6); Table 3 and Discussion, 2nd paragraph (p. 8)
key_findings.note: Table 3 and the Discussion list four trials with indirect effects (Dvorak 2015, Kenney 2014, LaBrie 2015, Larimer 2007); see reporting issues.

reporting_issues.issue: In the PRISMA diagram the database counts (PubMed 94, Embase 237, Scopus 117, CINAHL 71, ProQuest 45) sum to 564, but the total is printed as 514; the following boxes (58 duplicates, 456 screened) follow 514.
reporting_issues.consequence: Either a database count or the total is wrong; 50 records are unaccounted for, which weakens the audit trail of the search. (Fig. 1 has no text layer; counts read from the rendered page.)

reporting_issues.issue: The results text says three trials were at high risk of bias and describes overall risk of bias as low to moderate, but Fig. 2 shows four trials at high risk overall, ten at some concerns and one at low risk.
reporting_issues.consequence: The text understates the risk of bias of the evidence; claims should use the figure (14 of 15 trials at some concerns or high risk).

reporting_issues.issue: Arazan et al. (2023) has 88% to 95% attrition and 658 of 9,277 analysed (Table 1), yet its missing-outcome-data domain is judged low risk in Fig. 2.
reporting_issues.consequence: At least one domain judgment looks lenient, and this trial contributes to the problems and PBS-use pools.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 gives analysed numbers equal to randomized numbers for Braitman and Lau-Barraco 2018 (537/537 with 70–79% attrition), Braitman 2022 (528/528 with 31–45%), Larimer 2007 (1,488/1,488 with 33%) and Martens 2013 (365/365 with 5–6%).
reporting_issues.consequence: These trials presumably analysed all randomized participants with missing-data methods, but the review does not say which numbers and means entered its pooled post-intervention comparisons.

reporting_issues.issue: The results text reports significant indirect effects through PBS in three of six mediation trials, while Table 3 and the Discussion list four (Dvorak 2015, Kenney 2014, LaBrie 2015, Larimer 2007). Table 2 gives no mechanism test for Braitman 2022, Table 3 a non-significant moderation test. Table 3 marks Larimer 2007's PBS change as not assessed while concluding that its effects were mediated by increased PBS use.
reporting_issues.consequence: The narrative synthesis of mechanism cannot be reconciled with the tables; the count of trials supporting mediation is three or four depending on the source.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says eight trials showed clear increases in PBS use, but Table 3 marks nine as 'Yes' (with one mixed and one maintained, giving the stated eleven); the text says eleven interventions combined all three strategy domains, but Table 2 lists two of them (Andersson 2015; Arazan 2023) with two domains.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor counting errors in the descriptive synthesis.

reporting_issues.issue: Five trials had three to five arms (Table 1), but the review does not say which arms were compared or whether control groups were split, and the subgroup analysis prespecified as core/primary versus adjunct/booster (p. 3) is reported as adjunct versus core or primary without saying where the three booster trials went (p. 7).
reporting_issues.consequence: The pooled and subgroup estimates cannot be reproduced from the paper, and the adjunct subgroup's composition is unclear.

verification.source_read: PDF (version of record), Psychiatry Research 365 (2026) 117430, pp. 1–13 (all pages including declarations, funding and references; text extracted and checked on pages rendered at 150 dpi; Tables 1–3 checked on the rendered pages; Figs 1–6 read from the rendered page and the extracted figure images, forest-plot values legible and read from them). Supplementary material (Appendix 1 search strategy, Appendix 2 excluded studies, Supplementary Figs S1–S16) not among the files and not read.
